title: The Gothic Dancer, Brussels to Ascona: the Temple of Dance at San Materno
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Brussels, the house of the silk merchant
stops.campa: Charlotte Bachrach is born on 20 April in Brussels, daughter of Paul Bachrach, a German-Jewish silk merchant grown wealthy in the fabric trade, and of his wife Elvira. The house is no ordinary merchant's house: Heinrich Vogeler of Worpswede, master of the Jugendstil, has a hand in its rooms, so the child opens her eyes among drawn lilies and stained light. Silk, the moth's thread, is the family element; the daughter will spend her life making cloth move like spirit.
suggested_refs: Heinrich Vogeler, Portrait of the Dancer Charlotte Bara

stops.name: Brussels, the first lessons with Jeanne Defaw
stops.campa: At six years old Charlotte is given to Jeanne Defaw, a Belgian pupil of Isadora Duncan, and the barefoot gospel enters her body before any other creed. Defaw teaches the Duncan liberty: no barre, no blocked shoe, the arm lifted as the soul lifts, and the grave little girl takes to it not as play but as devotion. Watchers already note the strange stillness of her face when she moves, as of a child listening to something in the next room.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the child Charlotte Bachrach, Fondo Charlotte Bara, Museo comunale d'arte moderna, Ascona

stops.name: Brussels, the stone saints of Sainte-Gudule
stops.campa: In the cathedral of Saint Michael and Saint Gudula the girl stands before the stone saints and finds the alphabet she will spend her life spelling: the long praying hands, the grave inclined head, the body folded like a wing. From the Gothic sculptors and the Flemish painters of heaven she takes her whole grammar: not steps but attitudes of the soul. Years later the Berlin critics will say she discovered the soul of the Gothic entirely for herself; it is here that it discovers her.
suggested_refs: Cathedral of St. Michael and St. Gudula, Brussels, the Gothic portal sculpture

stops.name: Brussels, the war takes the house
stops.campa: On 20 August the German army enters Brussels. The Bachrachs, German Jews in a Belgian capital at war with Germany, are suddenly enemies in their own house: the property is confiscated, the silk business seized, and the family must go. Charlotte, thirteen, leaves the city of Defaw's lessons and the stone saints with what can be carried. The war that unhouses her also delivers her, for the road of exile runs north to a painter's hill she will remember as a refuge.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the German entry into Brussels, August 1914

stops.name: Worpswede, the Barkenhoff of Heinrich Vogeler
stops.campa: Charlotte and her mother come to rest at the Barkenhoff, Heinrich Vogeler's birch-hung house at Worpswede on the moor above Bremen: the family's old friend, the artist of their Brussels rooms, now their shelter. The colony of painters takes the grave Belgian child in among its canvases and peat-black canals. In the enormous northern light she goes on dancing, teaching herself, working the Gothic attitudes into a discipline no school gives her. Vogeler will paint her portrait; the moor keeps her; the war stays outside the birches.
suggested_refs: The Barkenhoff, Worpswede, Heinrich Vogeler's Jugendstil house, now his museum

stops.name: Brussels, the debut of the sixteen-year-old
stops.campa: In 1917, in occupied Brussels, Charlotte gives her first public evening of dances. She is sixteen. The city of her childhood, hungry and garrisoned, watches a girl perform grave sacred attitudes out of the thirteenth century as though the cathedral porch had stepped down and begun to move. It is a strange debut, wartime, a borrowed hall, an audience wrapped in coats, and it is remembered as the beginning: from this night she is a dancer publicly, and the family's ruin has produced its answer.
suggested_refs: Early recital photographs, Fondo Charlotte Bara, Ascona

stops.name: Worpswede: Carl Weidemeyer, the builder to come
stops.campa: At Worpswede in 1918 the Bachrachs meet Carl Weidemeyer of Bremen, painter and graphic artist of the colony, not yet an architect. Nothing is built; everything is founded. Ten years on, this acquaintance of the moor will raise for Charlotte the white temple of dance at Ascona, the first modern chamber theater in Switzerland. The canon loves such seeds: on the same birch hill, in the last year of the war, the dancer, her patron father and her future architect stand for a moment in one room.
suggested_refs: Carl Weidemeyer's Worpswede graphics; his later sketches of Charlotte Bara

segments.name: Holland and Berlin, the Gothic Dancer Made

stops.name: Rotterdam, the Dutch evenings
stops.campa: With the Armistice the borders open and Charlotte carries her dances into the Netherlands, giving evenings at Rotterdam and then Amsterdam through the winter. The Dutch, connoisseurs of the devotional image, receive the gothic dances warmly: the death-dance attitudes, the Egyptian friezes set moving, the praying figures that seem stepped down from an altarpiece. She is seventeen and touring on her own name. The critics reach for painters, not dancers, to describe her: a living sculpture, a panel come down from the altar and walking.
suggested_refs: Dutch recital programs, 1918-1919, Fondo Charlotte Bara

stops.name: The Hague: Raden Mas Jodjana, the hand-language
stops.campa: In Holland she finds the second of her masters: Raden Mas Jodjana, the Javanese prince, in her own estimation the finest mystical dancer alive. From him she learns the language of hands: the fingers as syllables, the wrist as breath, the gesture that speaks without translating. It is the East laid beside her Gothic and found to be the same tongue: dance as worship, the body as temple furniture. Later Uday Shankar, pioneer of the modern dance of India, will complete the oriental initiation.
stops.quote_source: Bara's recorded estimation of Jodjana, cited in the Dizionario della musica nella Svizzera italiana
suggested_refs: Photographs of Raden Mas Jodjana in dance costume, the Netherlands, c. 1919

stops.name: Amsterdam, the acclaim
stops.campa: Amsterdam confirms Rotterdam: full houses for the girl who dances saints. In these Dutch seasons the repertory that will carry her through Europe takes form: Vanité des Vanités, the Danse macabre, the mummy's dance, the Egyptian dance, the Hindu vision, the dying butterfly, each one a memento mori performed with the tenderness of a nun arranging flowers. The Netherlands, which schooled her in Jodjana's East, now sends her out as a name. Berlin is the next altar.
suggested_refs: Programs of Vanité des Vanités and Danza della mummia, Fondo Charlotte Bara

stops.name: Berlin, Max Reinhardt's Kammerspiele
stops.campa: Despite her youth she dances at the Kammerspiele of the Deutsches Theater, Max Reinhardt's chamber stage, and the Berlin critics, the hardest congregation in Europe, are won. In the capital of the new Ausdruckstanz, where Laban's pupils and Wigman's daimon are remaking the body, this Belgian girl arrives from a different century altogether, offering the twelfth. The press names her die gotische Tänzerin, the gothic dancer, and the name holds for life. Berlin will be her northern pole for a decade, with the Theater im Landwehrkasino following in 1920.
suggested_refs: Kammerspiele des Deutschen Theaters, Schumannstrasse, Berlin

stops.name: Berlin: Kolbe's portfolio, Meyer's little book
stops.campa: The sculptors claim her, as she claimed sculpture. Georg Kolbe, master of the dancing bronze, draws her oriental dances and publishes the sheets at Leipzig; Alfred Richard Meyer prints the first monograph, a slim Berlin hymn titled simply Charlotte Bara. At twenty she is a documented style: the sunken knee the academies scold, the lifted palms, the face of quiet blessedness. The Städel will keep a drawing of the dancer; the archive of her body accumulates in other artists' hands, since her art itself vanishes each evening.
suggested_refs: Georg Kolbe's portfolio of Charlotte Bara's oriental dances (Leipzig 1921)
A. R. Meyer, Charlotte Bara (Berlin 1921)

segments.name: Ascona, the Castle Below the Mountain

stops.name: Ascona, Castello San Materno
stops.campa: Paul Bachrach, who first saw the lake of Locarno on a holiday in 1910 and never forgot it, buys the Castello San Materno above Ascona, once a summer house of the canons of Milan cathedral, and sets the architect Paul Rudolf Henning to enlarge it. In 1920 the family settles for good. Charlotte writes north to Vogeler of the magnolias and amaryllis flowering at her new door. In the castle's great hall she begins at once to dance for invited guests: the castle is her first theater.
suggested_refs: Castello San Materno, Ascona, today the Museo Castello San Materno

stops.name: Monte Verità, the inherited mountain
stops.campa: Above her castle rises Monte Verità, the mountain of truth, where the life-reformers went barefoot and Rudolf Laban kept his dance farm in the summers before the war. By the time Charlotte climbs it the magus is gone north; she never stands in his studio, and the canon keeps the distinction clean. Yet the hill and the dancer belong to one story: his line will reach her by descent through Wigman's pupils in Berlin, and Ascona now has, in the castle below the hill, a second consecrated body.
suggested_refs: Casa Anatta, Monte Verità; Johann Adam Meisenbach's photographs of the Laban school, 1913-14

stops.name: Locarno: the Kursaal, first Ticino recital
stops.campa: Her first appearance before her new countrymen: an evening at the Teatro Kursaal in Locarno, dancing to Chopin, Grieg and Granados. The Ticinese, who know the Ascona hill mostly as a rumor of vegetarians and anarchists, discover instead a grave young woman performing the attitudes of their own church porches: adoration, lamentation, the folded hands of the stone Madonnas. The region adopts her; for the next thirty-six years the shore between Locarno and Ascona is her parish.
suggested_refs: The Kursaal of Locarno, later the Casinò, on the lakefront

stops.name: Berlin, Cürlis turns the camera
stops.campa: At the Institut für Kulturforschung in Berlin, Hans Cürlis, pioneer of the culture-film, sets his camera before her and records twelve minutes of the gothic dances. It is among the earliest attempts to give the new dance a body that outlives the evening. The film is later lost: the fate the canon assigns to almost everything she made, an art of attitudes surviving only in bronze, drawings and print. The dancer who took her grammar from things that last a thousand years leaves moving images that last thirty.
suggested_refs: Hans Cürlis's Institut für Kulturforschung film series 'Schaffende Hände', the lost 1923 Bara reel

stops.name: Locarno, the Festa delle Camelie
stops.campa: At the camellia festival of Locarno she gives her first mimed spectacle for the region: Il trionfo della camelia, verses by Silvio Sganzini, scenes and costume by Alexandre Cingria, Leo Kok at the piano. Before the assembled lake she performs the blossoming of a camellia: the closed bud, the slow unclenching, the full flower offered and then let fall. It is botany as theology, the resurrection argued by a flower, and the crowd on the lakefront understands it without a word of doctrine.
suggested_refs: Alexandre Cingria's camellia costume design for Charlotte Bara, 1924

segments.name: The Vittoriale, the Poet's Santa Ballerina

stops.name: Gardone Riviera, summoned to the Vittoriale
stops.campa: In 1924 Gabriele d'Annunzio, new-made Prince of Montenevoso, calls her to the Vittoriale on Lake Garda, and the gothic dancer performs her Egyptian and Hindu compositions and the dances of the cathedrals for the Comandante among his relics. He is taken above all by her hands, spiritual hands, and names her the santa ballerina, the holy dancer. 'Elle sait par quels mystères surgissent des profondeurs les plus belles clartés,' he writes: she knows by what mysteries the fairest lights rise out of the deepest places.
suggested_refs: Il Vittoriale degli Italiani, Gardone Riviera, the Prioria and the amphitheater

stops.name: The Vittoriale, the dance invented in a dream
stops.campa: The poet dreams for her. 'J'ai inventé une danse pour vous dans cette nuit en rêve,' he tells her, I invented a dance for you this night, in a dream, and assigns her titles as a poet assigns relics: La dernière colonne du Temple, the last column of the Temple; L'Arbre séraphique et les Oiseaux du ciel, the seraphic tree and the birds of heaven. He intends through her a total sacred artwork, as once with Debussy and Ida Rubinstein: his visions danced, conceivable only on mystical ground.
suggested_refs: D'Annunzio's letters and dedications to Charlotte Bara, Vittoriale archives

stops.name: The Vittoriale, Malipiero at the poet's table
stops.campa: Two years on, d'Annunzio summons her again, and at the Vittoriale sets her before Gian Francesco Malipiero, meaning to yoke the composer to the santa ballerina and give the dreamed dances their music. The commission is never realized, the canon's shelf of unbuilt temples receives it, but the meeting bears late fruit: Malipiero's music will carry her Eitelkeit–Vergänglichkeit on the Ascona stage for twenty years. From the lake of the Comandante she returns to her own lake, where her father is preparing the ground of her real temple.
suggested_refs: Gian Francesco Malipiero's scores of the 1920s; the Vittoriale music room

segments.name: The Capitals: Paris, the Rhine, Magdeburg, Rome

stops.name: Paris, the Comédie des Champs-Élysées
stops.campa: Paris debut at the Comédie des Champs-Élysées, the chamber stage in Perret's concrete temple where the Sacre rioted thirteen years before. The French critics of the dance, Fernand Divoire at their head, take her into the canon of the mystics; Divoire will fix her in Pour la danse among the figures of the age. Paris names what Berlin named, in its own tongue: a dancer not of the theater but of the cathedral, the gothic dancer, sister to the carved saints of the portals.
suggested_refs: Théâtre and Comédie des Champs-Élysées, avenue Montaigne, Paris

stops.name: Bad Godesberg, the Rhine seasons
stops.campa: Through 1926 and 1927 she dances at Bad Godesberg on the Rhine, in the Germany of the dance's great ferment. These are working seasons, the recital circuit of spa halls and city theaters by which the soloists of Ausdruckstanz lived, and they set her among her generation: Wigman's ecstatics, Laban's movement choirs, the Sacharoffs' painted legends. Against all of them Bara holds her single note, the sacred attitude, and the note carries. The gothic dancer is now a fixture of the German stage.
suggested_refs: Bad Godesberg Stadthalle recital programs, 1926-27

stops.name: Berlin, the school of Trümpy and Skoronel
stops.campa: In Berlin she perfects her craft at the school of Berthe Trümpy and Vera Skoronel: Trümpy who was Mary Wigman's pupil and right hand, Skoronel who was Trümpy's. Thus the lineage the canon is careful about: Laban begat Wigman, Wigman begat Trümpy, and through the Trümpy school the magus's method at last touches the gothic dancer, by descent, never by his hand. What Ascona's hill could not give her directly, Berlin gives her at two removes: the discipline of the new dance set beneath her old attitudes.
suggested_refs: The Trümpy-Skoronel school, Berlin; photographs of Berthe Trümpy and Vera Skoronel

stops.name: Magdeburg, the First German Dancers' Congress
stops.campa: June 1927: the whole church of the new dance assembles at Magdeburg for the first Deutscher Tänzerkongress, Laban and Wigman at the altar, the schools quarreling like orders of friars, and Charlotte Bara takes part. It is the one documented room that holds her and Laban together: a congress, not a collaboration, and the canon keeps the measure exact. Among the theorists and the ecstatics she stands for the third way of Ausdruckstanz: not the tragic, not the gymnastic, but the liturgical.
suggested_refs: Deutsche Theaterausstellung Magdeburg 1927, congress photographs and proceedings

stops.name: Ascona, the marriage to Carl Rütters
stops.campa: In 1927 she marries Carl Rütters, a psychiatrist: a reader of interiors, fit consort for a dancer of the interior life. He draws her again and again, adding his sheets to Kolbe's and Weidemeyer's; the archive of her body accumulates by loving hands. The marriage roots her the more firmly at San Materno, where the ground beside the castle is already staked out: her father has commissioned Weidemeyer, the friend of Worpswede, and the temple of dance is beginning to rise among the magnolias.
suggested_refs: Carl Rütters's drawings of Charlotte Bara, Fondo Charlotte Bara, Ascona

stops.name: Berlin: the Catholic evening, the critic's verdict
stops.campa: At a Catholic educational evening in Berlin she dances the Totentanz and the sacred attitudes, and the Berliner Zeitung delivers the sentence the canon keeps: she has discovered the soul of the Gothic entirely for herself. The critic adds, half in wonder, that had she danced these dances in the actual Middle Ages she would have burned for them as a witch. It is meant as a flourish; it is in fact her theology stated exactly: the Gothic not revived but re-entered, at personal risk.
suggested_refs: Berliner Zeitung review, February 1928 (Deutsches Tanzarchiv Köln, Bestand 147)

stops.name: Rome, Bragaglia's Una santa ballerina
stops.campa: Her Italian tours, Milan, Florence, Venice, Rome, win her the avant-garde's chronicler: Anton Giulio Bragaglia, futurist of the camera and impresario of the Independents, who this year prints Scultura vivente with a chapter that canonizes her under d'Annunzio's own word, Una santa ballerina: Carlotta Bara. Living sculpture: Bragaglia's title is her method read backward, the Gothic statue that learned to move. Italy files her beside its own mystics; the holy dancer now has her act of the saints in print.
suggested_refs: A. G. Bragaglia, Scultura vivente (Milan 1928), chapter 'Una santa ballerina: Carlotta Bara'

stops.name: Ascona, Weidemeyer raises the Teatro San Materno
stops.campa: In the castle park Carl Weidemeyer builds her theater, 1927 into 1928: flat roofs, white reinforced concrete, great glass toward the lake, the first chamber theater of the modern movement in Switzerland, a rationalist temple standing on the site of the old Romanesque church of San Materno. She conceives it as stage, school and dwelling in one body: a dance temple as the sublimation of a new form of life. The composer James Simon of Berlin directs the music teaching. The seed of Worpswede, planted 1918, is built.
stops.quote: the school's aim is training in the expressive dance of the inner conditions of the soul
stops.quote_source: The prospectus of Bara's school at the Teatro San Materno, quoted in the Dizionario della musica nella Svizzera italiana
suggested_refs: Teatro San Materno, Via Losone 3, Ascona, Carl Weidemeyer, 1927-28

stops.name: Ascona, the convert
stops.campa: In the year her temple opens she is received into the Catholic Church. The conversion surprises no one who has watched her dance: she has been performing the faith's attitudes since girlhood, and the baptism only signs what the body long confessed. The Jewish silk merchant's daughter becomes a Catholic dancer of the Gothic in a Swiss village: the canon delights in the braid. With the Benedictine teachers of the Collegio Papio she is already at home, dancing Scarlatti in their theater; sacred dance now has, in her, both its stage and its communicant.
suggested_refs: The Collegio Papio and church of Santa Maria della Misericordia, Ascona

stops.name: Einsiedeln, the round of angels
stops.campa: Her friendships among the Benedictine educators bear liturgical fruit: for Calderón's Great Theatre of the World, played before the abbey facade at Einsiedeln, she choreographs the Ridda degli angeli, the round of the angels. On the largest sacred stage in Switzerland, the square of the Black Madonna, thousands seated in the open night, her attitudes are multiplied into a wheeling angelic choir. The gothic dancer's grammar proves it can scale from solo to host; the church that once would have burned the dance now processes with it.
suggested_refs: The Einsiedeln Welttheater, Calderón's Gran Teatro del Mundo before the abbey facade

stops.name: Ascona, the guests of San Materno
stops.campa: The white theater becomes a famous small lamp of the Ticino. Jodjana dances there, and Tatiana Barbakoff; Sascha Leontjew; the eurythmy ensemble comes down from the Goetheanum. The musicians are unreasonable for a village: the Busch Quartet, Claudio Arrau, Rudolf Serkin. Two or three times a year Bara herself dances, indoors or on the open terrace above the lake, in her grave tunics. Marco Enrico Bossi had dreamed an American tour of her sacred dances to his organ; his sudden death at sea had left it dreamed.
suggested_refs: Teatro San Materno guest programs, 1928-1939, Fondo Charlotte Bara

stops.name: Ascona, Eitelkeit–Vergänglichkeit
stops.campa: She creates Eitelkeit–Vergänglichkeit, Vanity and Passing, on the San Materno stage, to the music of Malipiero: the Vittoriale meeting redeemed at last on her own ground. It is the mature statement of her oldest theme, the vanitas danced: the mirror, the flower, the skull, the slow surrender of the flesh to time performed by a body in absolute command of its own slowness. She will revive it in 1935, in 1937 and in 1951: a work about transience, faithfully kept for twenty years.
suggested_refs: Eitelkeit–Vergänglichkeit programs, Teatro San Materno, 1932-1951

stops.name: Ascona: the Flight into Egypt, with Leontjew
stops.campa: With Sascha Leontjew she stages Flucht nach Ägypten, the Flight into Egypt, her Gothic and her Egypt finally seated in one work: the Holy Family fleeing out of the Christian iconography into the land of the friezes she has danced since Holland. Europe in 1936 gives the subject its shadow; on the Swiss shore of a darkening continent, the dancer performs flight, refuge, the child carried to safety. Within a few years the theater itself will play the Egypt of the parable, and shelter the fleeing in earnest.
suggested_refs: Flucht nach Ägypten, Teatro San Materno, 1936, photographs with Sascha Leontjew

segments.name: The War, the Theater of Refuge

stops.name: Ascona: the theater goes dark, the doors open
stops.campa: The war closes the stage: through the conflict and long after, no dances at San Materno. But the canon records the greater performance: through the war years the theater's rooms house refugees and the persecuted. The daughter of confiscated Brussels, herself Jewish-born on the last safe shore, turns the temple of dance into what temples are for: sanctuary. The Flight into Egypt, danced in 1936, is now enacted in the corridors, nightly, unlit and unreviewed. It is the longest-running work her theater ever carried.
suggested_refs: Teatro San Materno, the dwelling wing that housed the persecuted, 1939-1952

stops.name: Auschwitz, the fate of the music master
stops.campa: The war reaches in and takes its due from the school itself: James Simon, the Berlin composer who directed the music teaching at San Materno, deported first to Theresienstadt, is carried in October 1944 to Auschwitz and murdered. The canon sets this stone in her itinerary because her temple's music had his hands in it; every later evening of sacred dance at Ascona carries this silence in the continuo. Of the school for expressive form, one master goes where no expression returns.
suggested_refs: James Simon (1880-1944), composer, Theresienstadt and Auschwitz memorial records

stops.name: Ascona, the Swiss citizen
stops.campa: After the war Switzerland gives her its passport. The stateless arc of the century, Belgian-born, German-blooded, unhoused in 1914, resettled in 1920, closes at last in the smallest and safest of nations: Charlotte Bara, Swiss citizen of Ascona. The theater remains dark, as if observing a mourning; the dancer is forty-five and unhurried. In the castle she keeps her tunics, her programs, her instruments. What returns to a stage after such a war must return as liturgy, and she prepares it deliberately.
suggested_refs: Naturalization records, commune of Ascona

segments.name: The Domestic Liturgy, and the Long Evening

stops.name: Ascona, Danses sacrées de l'Orient
stops.campa: The first light after the dark decade: Danses sacrées de l'Orient, the sacred dances of the East, at San Materno in 1950. She reopens with Jodjana's inheritance, the hand-language, the temple gestures, as though the way back to the Gothic led properly through Egypt, the route of the Holy Family reversed. The audiences are smaller, the shore quieter, the century elsewhere; none of it signifies. The theater relights on her own terms: dance as devotion, offered at intervals, to whom it concerns.
suggested_refs: Danses sacrées de l'Orient program, Teatro San Materno, 1950

stops.name: Ascona: the wise and foolish virgins, with Olga Schwind
stops.campa: The true reopening, 1952: an evening of early music and medieval sacred dance with Olga Schwind of Ronco sopra Ascona, lutenist and organist of the old repertories: La resurrezione delle vergini stolte e sagge, the resurrection of the wise and foolish virgins, and La danza dei beati, the dance of the blessed, after Dante. Two women past the world's fashion restore the Middle Ages on a rationalist stage, exactly, unhurriedly, and the Asconesi remember it for decades: medieval dance made gesture full of enigmas.
suggested_refs: Olga Schwind (1887-1979) with her early instruments, lute, portative organ

stops.name: Ascona, the Easter liturgy of San Materno
stops.campa: Now the theater's calendar is the Church's: in the days before and after Easter she gives her sacred dances almost as a domestic liturgy, with small consorts of old instruments: vielle, portative organ, Minnesänger harp, pan flute, and amateur companions where needed. In 1955 she dances Zu Ehren von Fra' Angelico, in honor of Fra Angelico, to César Franck, and revives the Flight into Egypt. The gothic dancer has become what she always imitated: a fixed feast, a local rite, an image before which the faithful gather annually.
stops.quote: Dance is the most complete prayer, for the sense and the intensity of the gesture have no equal in the word
stops.quote_source: Bara on her sacred dances, recorded in the Dizionario della musica nella Svizzera italiana
suggested_refs: Zu Ehren von Fra' Angelico, Teatro San Materno, 1955, program and photographs

stops.name: Ascona, the last dance
stops.campa: In July 1958 Charlotte Bara dances at San Materno for the last time. No abdication scene is recorded; the liturgy simply completes itself, thirty years almost to the season since the white theater opened. She is fifty-seven and has danced publicly for forty-one years: Brussels under occupation, Reinhardt's Berlin, the poet's lake, her own temple. The stage falls quiet; the school closes its register; the castle keeps her. The long evening of the dancer begins, which the canon counts not as silence but as stillness.
suggested_refs: The last recital programs, Teatro San Materno, July 1958

stops.name: Monte Verità: Szeemann's mountain, the elder witness
stops.campa: Harald Szeemann raises his great exhibition Monte Verità, le mammelle della verità, across Ascona, Casa Anatta and the Brissago islands, and sets Charlotte Bara among its exemplary artists: the hill's whole heresy curated as a total artwork, and the gothic dancer, seventy-seven and living below in her castle, entered into the museum of her own myth beside Laban and the barefoot prophets she outlived. The same year the theater passes to the commune of Ascona. She attends her own canonization with the composure of one who always knew the Gothic outlasts its century.
suggested_refs: Harald Szeemann, Monte Verità: le mammelle della verità (exhibition, 1978); Casa Anatta

stops.name: Locarno, the death of the gothic dancer
stops.campa: She dies at Locarno on 7 December 1986, eighty-five years old, having lived out her days at San Materno among the drawings, programs and tunics of six decades. The obituaries reach back to the twenties to explain her; the lake needs no explanation, having kept her as a neighbor saint for sixty-six years. Of the great soloists of Ausdruckstanz she is among the last to go: the one who answered the century's ecstasies and catastrophes with a single sustained attitude of adoration.
suggested_refs: Charlotte Bara's late portraits and obituaries, Fondo Charlotte Bara, Ascona

stops.name: Ascona, the temple dances again
stops.campa: The afterlife of the temple: the canton lists Weidemeyer's white geometry among its protected monuments, the commune restores it with archaeological care, and the Teatro San Materno reopens as a working theater of dance. In 2007 her archive, more than two thousand four hundred photographs, letters and programs, enters the museums of Ascona; in 2018 Roberta Pedrini's film Le passioni di Charlotte carries her to the screens. A school of dance keeps term on the site once more; the twelve minutes the century lost in 1923 are thus, in kind, repaid.
suggested_refs: Teatro San Materno restored (2006-2009), Ascona; Roberta Pedrini, Le passioni di Charlotte (2018)
